transcript.text: w/m finally died after 12 yrs, whats the best one to buy under £400? family of 5

For a family of five, I’d aim for a 9–10 kg, 1400 rpm washing machine rather than the cheapest 7–8 kg model. Under £400, the best-value target is usually a simple 9 kg machine from a mainstream brand with a good UK service network, a proper quick wash, delay start, and a high-spin option. Avoid paying extra mainly for Wi-Fi, steam or very complex auto-dose features at this budget — capacity, a decent warranty and available servicing matter more. A practical shortlist specification:
1. 9 kg minimum; 10 kg if you regularly wash bedding, towels and school/sports kit.
2. 1400 rpm spin, to reduce drying time.
3. Standard detergent drawer and straightforward controls.
4. Check the delivered price, removal of the old machine, installation, and warranty terms — these can change which deal is actually best. It may still be worth checking the old one first. “Died” can be a failed socket/circuit, door lock, blocked drain, or control fault; not all of those justify replacement after 12 years. With the machine switched off, check the plug and socket by trying another known-working appliance in that socket, and check whether the consumer-unit breaker has tripped. Then switch the washer back on and try a normal programme. If it is completely blank, power supply/control is more likely; if it lights up but will not start, the door lock or drain side rises up the list; a displayed code would narrow it quickly.
it does power on, stops mid-cycle with water in drum, won't drain or spin. hums when it tries to drain. some lights flashing, dont know which. would repair if cheap

This points to a drainage fault, not a spin or motor fault: the washer will normally refuse to spin while water is still in the drum. A kinked hose/waste blockage is next; only after those are ruled out does the drain pump itself become likely. 1. Switch it off, unplug it, and allow any hot wash water to cool. Put towels and a shallow tray at the bottom-front filter flap. If the manual shows an emergency drain hose, use that first; otherwise loosen the filter very slowly, stopping to empty the tray as water comes out. 2. Remove and clean the pump filter. Look for coins, hair grips, buttons, lint or fabric. With the filter out, use a torch and gently feel whether the small impeller behind it will turn; it may move in small steps, but it should not be solidly jammed or have broken vanes. 3. Check the drain hose at the back is not crushed or kinked, and that the connection to the standpipe/sink waste is not blocked. If water backs up from the household drain, that is a plumbing restriction rather than a washer part fault. Refit the filter securely, then try a drain or spin-only programme. If it drains normally, the fault was likely the blockage. If the filter and hose are clear but it still only hums and shifts no water, the drain pump is the leading suspect; that is usually a reasonable repair, but an engineer can confirm it before any part is fitted.
didn't know there was a filter tbh. its a Hotpoint WMBF944P, 12 yrs old. ok will unplug and have a look, anything else to watch for?

Yes — the main thing is to expect more water than you think. Put plenty of towels down and use a shallow tray; loosen the filter only a little at a time, then tighten it again while you empty the tray. If there is a small emergency-drain tube behind the flap, use that first. 1. Switch off and unplug before opening the flap. Do not run it with the filter removed.
2. Let any wash water cool first. Wear gloves if you are feeling into the opening: broken hair grips, pins or glass can be caught there.
3. Do not force the filter or the little impeller behind it. The impeller may turn in small steps, but if it is solidly jammed, or its vanes are damaged, stop rather than levering it.
4. Before refitting, wipe the filter seal and its seating clean. Screw it fully home by hand; a poorly seated filter can leak on the next drain.
5. Also look behind the machine for a crushed or sharply kinked drain hose, but do not pull the washer out alone if it is heavy or the hoses are tight. Water remaining in the drum and no spin makes a drainage blockage the leading possibility; the filter result will distinguish that from a hose restriction or a pump/internal blockage. If the filter is clear and the hose is not kinked, but it still will not empty after reassembly, that is the point to consider an appliance engineer rather than buying a part blind.
ok thanks, will unplug it and check the filter and hose. back in a bit

No problem. The filter and hose check is the right next step and may be a free fix. Keep the machine unplugged while you do it, and take the result one step at a time: anything found in the filter or around the impeller points to a blockage; a clear filter plus a sound, unrestricted hose makes the drain pump or an internal blockage more likely. Let me know what you find when you are back.
ok back. haven't actually checked yet, just about to. what should I do if there's loads of water?

If there is a lot of water, do not fully undo the filter in one go. Keep it unplugged, put a baking tray/shallow dish tight under the flap, and loosen the filter just enough for a controlled trickle. Tighten it again while you empty the tray, then repeat. Towels around the front will catch the inevitable spills. If there is a small emergency-drain tube behind the flap, use that instead: uncap it into a low tray, empty the tray repeatedly, then refit its cap before opening the filter. It can take quite a few trips if the drum is full. Do not try to tip the machine or pull the drain hose out of the standpipe with a full drum. If the water is hot, let it cool; gloves are sensible in case of pins, glass or hair grips. Once most of the water is out, remove the filter and check for debris and the small impeller just behind it. The leading possibilities remain a blocked filter/pump path, then a restricted hose/waste connection, or a pump that is jammed or failing. What you find at the filter is the best next separator.
